introduction: England's uneasy King Henry IV faces threats from the very nobles who helped him gain the crown. Their most admired young warrior, Hotspur, offers a troubling contrast to Henry's son Hal, whose days pass among tavern companions and thieves. As the Percys move towards rebellion, Hal's friendship with the exuberant Falstaff meets the demands of inheritance and war. Royal authority, military honour and comic self-invention compete to define what the Prince will become.

fullSynopsis.text: King Henry IV hopes to end England's civil strife with a crusade, but trouble at home intervenes. Mortimer has been captured by the Welsh leader Glendower, while Hotspur's Scottish victories make the King painfully conscious of his own son Hal's disreputable companions. Hotspur's reluctance to surrender his prisoners brings the Percys into conflict with Henry. When the King refuses to ransom Mortimer, whom he calls a traitor, Worcester and Northumberland turn their grievances into rebellion. They have helped Henry displace Richard II and now fear the power they established.

Hal spends his time with Falstaff, a witty knight who combines affectionate familiarity with theft and extravagant self-excuse. Privately, however, the Prince intends his eventual reformation to shine against his present misconduct. He and Poins arrange to rob Falstaff and his accomplices after those men rob travellers at Gadshill. The trick succeeds, and Falstaff's account of fighting overwhelming numbers collapses when Hal reveals what happened. Falstaff immediately claims that instinct prevented him from attacking the true Prince. Meanwhile, Hotspur ignores a cautious correspondent and evades his wife's anxious questions about his preparations.

News of the rebellion interrupts the tavern merriment. Hal and Falstaff rehearse the coming royal interview, taking turns as King and Prince; when Falstaff pleads for himself, Hal's assumed king promises banishment. Hal nevertheless protects him from the sheriff. Among the rebels, Mortimer, Glendower and Hotspur plan to divide the kingdom. Hotspur's quarrels over the map and Glendower's supernatural boasts expose strains within their alliance. Mortimer and his Welsh wife communicate through affection despite their different languages, while Hotspur remains impatient with domestic delay. Worcester warns that his nephew's abrasive pride can alienate friends.

Henry rebukes Hal for cheapening his royal standing and compares him unfavourably with Hotspur. The Prince promises to redeem his reputation in combat with his rival, winning a renewed share in his father's military trust. Back at the tavern, he exposes Falstaff's false accusations against the hostess, announces that the stolen money has been repaid, and sends his companions towards the war. Falstaff abuses his recruiting commission by accepting payments from men who buy exemption, replacing them with impoverished and ill-equipped recruits whom he dismisses as expendable.

The rebels gather near Shrewsbury without Northumberland, reportedly sick, or Glendower, whose forces cannot arrive in time; Mortimer is also absent. Hotspur answers these losses with confidence and resents reports of Hal's impressive military appearance. Blunt brings offers of redress and pardon, and Hotspur agrees to send Worcester to the King. Henry renews the offer, while Hal proposes single combat to spare the armies. Worcester fears that reconciliation would leave the older conspirators vulnerable to future punishment. He therefore conceals the pardon from Hotspur and falsely represents the King as refusing mercy, helping to precipitate the battle.

At Shrewsbury, Douglas kills Blunt, who wears the King's likeness, and later endangers Henry himself. Wounded Hal refuses to withdraw, rescues his father and kills Hotspur in single combat. Falstaff survives Douglas by pretending to be dead, then wounds Hotspur's corpse and claims the victory. Hal knows the claim is false but offers to embellish it. The royal army wins, and Henry sends Worcester and Vernon to execution. Hal orders the captured Douglas released without ransom, giving John the honour of conveying his freedom. Henry and his sons prepare separate campaigns against the remaining rebels: the victory has restored Hal's standing, but has not ended the conflict.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Henry's proposed crusade gives way to unrest in Wales and a quarrel with the Percys over Scottish prisoners. Reports of Hotspur's victories sharpen his disappointment in Hal, who jokes with Falstaff about drinking, theft and the privileges of a future king. Poins recruits Hal into a plan to expose Falstaff's cowardice by robbing the robbers after their Gadshill attack. Alone, Hal reveals his intention to surprise the world with a calculated reformation. At court, Hotspur defends his conduct and demands Mortimer's ransom; Henry treats Mortimer's Welsh marriage as evidence of treachery and refuses. The angry Percys recall their part in Henry's rise and Mortimer's prior designation as Richard's heir. Worcester directs their resentment towards a coalition with the Scots, Glendower and the Archbishop of York, while Hotspur welcomes the prospect of action.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: An inn's chamberlain supplies Gadshill with information about wealthy travellers. Falstaff and his companions rob them, only to flee when Hal and Poins attack in disguise and take the proceeds. At Warkworth, Hotspur dismisses a correspondent's doubts about the conspiracy and evades Lady Percy's questions about his distracted, warlike behaviour. In Eastcheap, Hal teases a drawer before Falstaff returns with an expanding tale of heroic resistance. Exposed, Falstaff substitutes an implausible claim to have recognized the Prince. A summons from court turns their games towards the rebellion: Hal and Falstaff impersonate father and son, and Hal's royal role answers Falstaff's plea against banishment with an ominous promise. When the sheriff arrives, Hal hides Falstaff, undertakes to answer for him, and finds the supposedly formidable knight asleep behind the curtain.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: The conspirators negotiate their proposed division of England and Wales, but Hotspur disputes a river boundary and mocks Glendower's claims to supernatural power. Mortimer and Worcester urge him to moderate his temper. The rebels pause for farewells to their wives, including a Welsh song from Lady Mortimer, whose language her husband cannot understand. In London, Henry confronts Hal with the damage his conduct has done to royal authority, contrasting it with his own carefully managed public presence and Hotspur's martial reputation. Hal promises to redeem himself by defeating Hotspur, and Henry entrusts him with a place in the campaign. At the tavern, Hal exposes Falstaff's accusations of theft against the hostess, reports that the robbery money has been repaid, and gives Falstaff and the others military employment.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Northumberland's reported illness deprives Hotspur's camp of his support; Vernon also brings news that Glendower cannot arrive for fourteen days. His praise of the transformed Prince of Wales provokes Hotspur's competitive anger. Worcester sees grave dangers in their reduced strength, but Hotspur turns every disadvantage into a reason for confidence. Falstaff, meanwhile, admits taking money from prosperous men to release them from military service, filling their places with destitute recruits. He treats their likely deaths with chilling indifference. The rebels disagree over whether to fight immediately. Blunt arrives with the King's offer to redress grievances and pardon them, and Hotspur arranges for Worcester to answer the following morning. At York, the Archbishop fears defeat at Shrewsbury and sends urgent messages to strengthen his own preparations against the King.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Henry offers general pardon, and Hal proposes settling his rivalry with Hotspur by single combat. Worcester withholds the pardon, fearing future punishment, and tells Hotspur that no mercy is available. As battle begins, Falstaff questions the value of honour, which cannot heal wounds; his recruits are virtually annihilated. Douglas kills Blunt in royal disguise and attacks the real King, whom Hal rescues. Hal then kills Hotspur while Falstaff feigns death to escape Douglas. Rising afterwards, Falstaff wounds Hotspur's corpse and claims the kill; Hal tolerates the lie. With the rebels defeated, Henry sends Worcester and Vernon to death. Hal directs that Douglas be released without ransom and lets John convey this courtesy. Henry divides his forces for further action against Northumberland and the Archbishop in the north, and Glendower and Mortimer in Wales.
